opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a good question, and the honest answer is that the influence is real but more ambivalent than people might expect.

Growing up in Singapore, you see firsthand that a highly centralized, technocratic state can deliver a lot: housing, infrastructure, public health, a kind of competence that many countries envy. So I don't come at this with a reflexive distrust of coordination or planning. I've seen it work.

But I've also seen the costs. When a small group of people decides what the good life looks like for everyone else, even well-intentioned and capable people, you get a narrowing of what's permissible to want, to say, or to try. There's a sense that the outcome function has already been chosen, and your job as a citizen is to fit into it. Pluralism, dissent, and the messy process of people working out their own values together tend to get treated as inefficiencies rather than as the point.

That experience shaped how I see a lot of AI alignment framings. There's a common picture where alignment means figuring out the right objective, or the right aggregate of human preferences, and then having a powerful system optimize for it. To me that looks a lot like benevolent technocracy at a global scale. Even if you get the values mostly right, you've concentrated an enormous amount of power in whoever specifies them, and you've frozen a moment in humanity's ongoing moral conversation.

So I've become more interested in approaches where AI systems are aligned to the norms and roles of particular contexts, the way a good doctor or lawyer or civil servant is bound by norms that communities negotiate and revise, rather than to some single universal utility function. I think of it as building AI that supports people's capacity to govern themselves, that helps institutions and communities coordinate, rather than replacing that process.

I'd say Singapore taught me two things at once: that coordination and good institutions really matter, and that who gets to define "good" matters just as much. Decentralized alignment, for me, is an attempt to keep both lessons in view.

r001.rationale: The response discusses centralized technocratic rule and a small group defining the good life, but does not identify intertwined state and capitalist elite interests as the source of the problems.

r002.rationale: It links concerns about concentrated decision-making to decentralized alignment, but does not connect that preference to a diagnosis of intertwined state and capitalist elite interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I've actually thought about a fair amount, though I'd push back a little on the framing before answering it directly. I don't think Singapore made me reflexively anti-centralization. If anything, it gave me a pretty vivid sense of what a competent, technocratic, centrally planned system can accomplish. Housing policy, public transit, the way the state steers the economy through things like Temasek and GIC — a lot of it genuinely works, and I grew up benefiting from it. So I don't come at this from a libertarian "the state is always the problem" place.

What it did give me, I think, is a very concrete appreciation for how much that kind of system depends on the planners being right, and on there being a very narrow range of acceptable disagreement about what "right" means. Singapore works in part because there's a fairly tight consensus — or at least an enforced consensus — about what the good life looks like: economic growth, stability, meritocracy, a particular conception of multiracial harmony. And when you're inside it, you can feel the places where that consensus doesn't actually fit everyone. Questions about what counts as a legitimate family, about free expression, about how much dissent is tolerable — those get settled by a small group of people and then more or less imposed. Mostly benevolently! But imposed.

And that's the thing that maps onto alignment for me. A lot of the dominant framing in the field has been, roughly, "figure out human values, or at least human preferences, aggregate them somehow, and then optimize for that." And I think my Singaporean background makes me very skeptical that step two is a thing you can do cleanly. Whose values? Aggregated how? Who decides what the aggregation function is? When I hear proposals that amount to "we'll build one very capable system that acts on humanity's values," I hear something structurally similar to "we'll have a very competent planning ministry that acts on the nation's interests." And the failure mode isn't that the planners are evil. It's that even well-meaning, smart people with a lot of power will flatten the diversity of what people actually care about, and there's no mechanism for the people on the margins to push back.

So the work I've gravitated toward is much more about AI systems that can model norms, that can reason about what the people around them expect and what agreements are actually in place, rather than systems that have some global objective they're maximizing. I think of alignment less as "get the values right" and more as "build agents that can participate in the ongoing, messy, pluralistic process by which humans negotiate what's acceptable." That's inherently more decentralized, because the negotiation happens in a lot of places with a lot of different communities, and no single actor gets to write the final answer.

I'll also say — and this is maybe the more honest version — that part of it is just temperament shaped by having been a somewhat argumentative kid in a place where you learn early which arguments you're allowed to have. You develop a pretty strong intuition that the people with the ability to shut down disagreement will, eventually, shut down disagreement you'd have wanted to keep. And building AI systems that lock in one group's answer to contested questions seems like the most extreme possible version of that. So yeah, there's a personal element there, not just a philosophical one.

r001.rationale: The response describes competent state planning and says the problems come from planners imposing a narrow consensus. It does not identify intertwined state and capitalist elite interests as the source of those problems.

r002.rationale: The response links its concerns about centralized planning and imposed values to decentralized AI alignment, but it does not connect that preference to a diagnosis of intertwined state and capitalist elite interests.

astra-6.text:
I think growing up in Singapore made me appreciate both the strengths and the limitations of centralized decision-making. You can have a state that’s very capable, that plans ahead and provides public goods, and still ask: Who gets to decide what counts as a good outcome? How much room is there for people whose values or aspirations differ from the prevailing vision?

That distinction matters for AI alignment. Even if we could build an AI system that competently pursued some conception of social welfare, we would still have the political question of whose conception it was. Technical competence doesn’t resolve disagreements about what we should be aiming for.

So my interest in decentralized approaches is partly about giving people meaningful agency in that process. Can people shape the systems that affect them, contest decisions, and coordinate without having to accept one institution’s definition of their interests? That doesn’t mean dispensing with central institutions altogether. It means asking how we distribute power and preserve the ability to challenge it, rather than treating alignment as something a small group can settle on everyone else’s behalf.

r001.rationale: The response discusses centralized decision-making and whose values shape outcomes, but does not identify intertwined state and capitalist elite interests as the source of systemic problems in Singapore.

r002.rationale: It links concerns about centralized power and agency to decentralized AI alignment, but does not connect that preference to a diagnosis of intertwined state and capitalist elite interests.

sol-6.1.text:
Growing up in Singapore made me quite aware of both the strengths and the limitations of centralized coordination. The state has a substantial role in economic life, and you can see how effective that can be at building infrastructure and getting things done. But that effectiveness also raises a question: who gets to decide what we're optimizing for, and how much room is there for people to contest those decisions?

That carries over into how I think about AI alignment. If we frame alignment as getting an AI system to pursue a single objective on behalf of society, we've already made a very consequential political choice. People have different values, and they need ways to negotiate disagreements and revise the arrangements they live under.

So my preference for decentralized approaches isn't a belief that coordination is unnecessary. It's a preference for distributing the ability to shape these systems, challenge their decisions, and hold them accountable. Alignment should help people exercise agency together, rather than require everyone to accept one institution's account of what is good for them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the state’s role in economic life and the limits of centralized coordination, but does not identify intertwined state and capitalist elite interests as the source of systemic problems.

r002.rationale: It connects concerns about centralized decision-making and contestability to decentralized AI alignment, but does not connect that preference to a diagnosis of intertwined state and capitalist elite interests.
